strengths: Optimizing incremental causal benefit rather than activation counts is a useful motivation. Allowing negative treatment effects also identifies an important limitation of conventional influence maximization.
The estimation-then-selection pipeline is understandable, and the nonnegative-effect special case connects naturally to established weighted influence-maximization results.

The Goodreads experiments report substantial gains over the selected baselines and include repeated runs, noise sensitivity, and runtime measurements. The reported public-data simulations raise no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The central approximation guarantee is not established. Appendix B, Eq. (6), incorrectly expresses influence as a sum of separate seed contributions, double-counting overlapping cascades: two zero-weight seeds that certainly activate the same unit-weight node contribute 1 to the objective, but 2 to this expression. Independently, Eq. (14) incorrectly bounds the accumulated error term: its coefficient is K(1-1/K)^K, which equals 0.889 for K=3, exceeding the claimed bound exp(1/K-1)=0.513. These substantive errors undermine Theorem 5.5.

The implemented CELF variant lacks justification for negative effects. CELF relies on submodularity to make previously computed marginal gains upper bounds. The manuscript explicitly acknowledges that signed effects can destroy submodularity, yet Algorithm 5 and the experiments retain standard lazy selection. Consequently, the implemented algorithm need not match full greedy, and a guarantee for full greedy would not automatically apply.

The causal estimand and identification argument are incomplete. Assumption 3.2 excludes outcome interference, while Section 4.1 models treatment-dependent interference from neighboring nodes. The manuscript does not reconcile these choices or explain why node effects estimated under observed neighboring treatments remain fixed when seed selection changes exposure. Positivity is not stated, and Proposition 3.6 contains the unfinished justification 'by assumption...'.

The robustness proof does not adequately handle signed objectives. Appendix C applies multiplicative inequalities whose direction can fail when objective values are negative. Relative-error assumptions also require treatment of zero-valued objectives and cancellation between positive and negative effects. No simulation sample-complexity analysis establishes the assumed uniform error control, so Theorem 5.7 does not substantiate the claimed practical robustness.

The diffusion process is inconsistent across the formulation and implementation. Section 3.1 describes independent-cascade activation through newly activated neighbors; Section 4.1 instead repeatedly selects one incident hyperedge, and Appendix A specifies an SI contact process. Their equivalence is not established. Algorithm 4 also uses T for both simulation repetitions and diffusion steps, confounding Monte Carlo accuracy with changes to the propagation horizon.

The evaluation does not validate the principal causal claims. It uses one approximately 4,400-node Goodreads subgraph with simulated treatment effects, rather than measured intervention outcomes. No reported effect-estimation accuracy, oracle-effect comparison, or alternative-estimator ablation establishes the benefit of recovering effects from observational data. Comparisons only with unweighted CELF and random selection cannot establish an advantage over existing weighted influence maximization. Noise-induced variance alone does not demonstrate preservation of expected utility or approximation quality.

The substantive novelty remains insufficiently supported. The causal estimator is adopted from [25], greedy and CELF are established algorithms, and weighted influence maximization is already acknowledged in [36]. The potentially distinguishing signed-effect guarantees have unresolved correctness problems, while no experiment isolates the benefit of hypergraph structure over an appropriate graph representation.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the reported claims. The manuscript provides no code link and insufficient detail about subgraph selection, covariates, treatment/outcome simulation parameters, estimator losses and training settings, and independent evaluation. It is also unclear whether selection and evaluation use estimated or simulated ground-truth effects. These omissions prevent reliable reconstruction and interpretation of the results.
